stated: The Conservative Party commits to cutting the main rate of employee National Insurance from 12% to 6% by April 2027, representing a total tax cut of £1,350 for the average worker on £35,000.

source.quote: Cut tax for workers by taking another 2p off employee National Insurance so that we will have halved it from 12% at the beginning of this year to 6% by April 2027, a total tax cut of £1,350 for the average worker on £35,000 – and the next step in our long-term ambition to end the double tax on work when financial conditions allow.

bearing_set.reason: Cutting employee NI directly raises workers' take-home pay, increasing real disposable income and ability to afford essentials — a core O2 indicator.
The cut raises net real wages for employees, directly bearing on whether workers can earn a decent, secure living — O4's primary indicator.

Directly raises employee take-home pay by cutting the main NI rate from 12% to 6%, with a concrete per-worker gain (£1,350/yr at £35k), affecting all employees between the primary threshold and upper earnings limit.

Halving the main employee NI rate removes a very large share of one of the UK's biggest revenue sources (employee Class 1 NI raises ~£100bn/yr); absent explicit funding offsets, this materially widens the structural deficit and worsens the debt path.

Gains are confined to employees earning above the primary threshold; pensioners, the unemployed, self-employed, and below-threshold workers receive nothing, and in absolute terms higher-paid employees gain more, producing a non-neutral distributional effect on the income gap.

membership_note: The primary bearing is O11 (take-home pay), with a major fiscal counterpart on O12 (unfunded revenue loss at scale) and a meaningful distributional effect on O14 (excluded groups and within-employee incidence). Macro labour-supply and O13 effects are second-order and too uncertain to clear the non-negligible bar separately.
